q: To send a continuous train of waves (not just a single pulse) along a stretched rope, the end of the rope must be:
o: Given one sharp jerk and then held still
Moved up and down repeatedly at a steady rate
x: A continuous wave needs a continuous source of vibration; each up-and-down cycle of the hand sends out one wavelength. A single jerk gives only a pulse.

q: A transverse wave travels along a stretched rope. At the instant a particle of the rope is at a crest, its velocity is:
x: At a crest the particle is at its maximum displacement, where it stops for an instant before moving back. Particles move fastest as they pass through the mean position.

q: When a longitudinal wave travels along a slinky spring, each coil of the spring:
o: Moves back and forth along the length of the spring about its own position
Moves steadily from the source to the far end
Moves up and down across the length of the spring
Stays completely still while the wave passes
x: In a longitudinal wave the coils vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, about their mean positions. Only the compressions, rarefactions and energy travel along the spring.

q: The tension in a stretched rope is increased while the hand shaking it keeps the same frequency. The waves on the rope will now have:
o: A greater speed and a shorter wavelength
The same speed and a longer wavelength
A smaller speed and a shorter wavelength
A greater speed and a longer wavelength
x: Wave speed on a rope is v = √(T/μ), so a larger tension gives a larger speed. With f fixed, λ = v/f also increases.

q: A wave travels along a light rope that is joined to a much heavier rope. As the wave passes into the heavier rope, which quantity stays the same?
x: The frequency is set by the source and cannot change at the join. The speed is smaller in the heavier rope, so the wavelength changes too.

q: A pulse travelling along a rope reaches an end that is tied firmly to a wall. The reflected pulse is:
o: Upright, with exactly the same shape
Inverted, so an upward pulse returns as a downward pulse
x: At a fixed end the rope cannot move, so the pulse is reflected inverted (a phase change of π). It travels back at the same speed.

q: A student moves one end of a long rope up and down 4 times per second. A crest is seen to travel 6 m along the rope in 2 s. The wavelength of the waves on the rope is:
x: Speed v = 6/2 = 3 m s⁻¹ and f = 4 Hz, so λ = v/f = 3/4 = 0.75 m. Dividing 6 m by 4 (1.5 m) forgets that the crest took 2 s.

q: Which of the following can travel through a vacuum?
x: X-rays are electromagnetic waves and need no medium. Sound, water waves and string waves are mechanical waves and need a material medium.

q: Mechanical waves cannot travel through a vacuum because they travel by:
o: Changes in electric and magnetic fields
A flow of matter from the source to the receiver
Vibrations of particles that pass the disturbance on to their neighbours
Heat passing from hot regions to cold regions
x: A mechanical wave is passed along by particles of the medium pushing and pulling on neighbouring particles. A vacuum has no particles, so the wave cannot be passed on.

q: For a mechanical wave to travel through a material, the material must have:
x: Elasticity gives the restoring force that pulls displaced particles back, and inertia (mass) makes them overshoot and pass the motion on. These properties of the medium carry mechanical waves.

q: Waves from an earthquake travel through the rocks of the Earth. These waves are:
o: Electromagnetic waves, because they travel very fast
Mechanical waves, because they need the rock as a medium
Electromagnetic waves, because they can cross empty space
x: Seismic waves are vibrations of the rock itself, so they are mechanical waves that need a medium. They cannot cross a vacuum.

q: A lightning flash is seen and the thunder is heard 3 s later. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ and treating the light as arriving instantly, the distance to the lightning is about:
x: Light, an electromagnetic wave, is so fast that its travel time is negligible. Distance = 340 × 3 = 1020 m.

q: A sound wave and a light wave both pass from air into water. Which statement is correct?
o: Sound speeds up, but light slows down
Sound slows down, but light speeds up
x: Sound, a mechanical wave, travels faster in water (about 1500 m s⁻¹) than in air (about 340 m s⁻¹). Light is fastest in a vacuum and slows down in water, which is optically denser than air.

q: Electromagnetic waves are produced by:
o: Vibrating particles of a material medium
Charges at rest in a strong field
x: An oscillating, and so accelerating, charge produces changing electric and magnetic fields that travel out as an electromagnetic wave. Charges at rest or in uniform motion do not radiate.

q: In a longitudinal wave, a rarefaction is a part of the medium in which:
o: The particles are closest together and the pressure is highest
The particles are farther apart and the pressure is lower than normal
The particles have their largest sideways displacement
There are no particles at all
x: A rarefaction is a stretched region: particles are spread out, so density and pressure fall below normal. The crowded, high-pressure region is a compression.

q: The SI unit of frequency, the hertz (Hz), is equivalent to:
x: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, so 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹. The second is the unit of time period, which is the reciprocal of frequency.

q: In a longitudinal wave, the distance from the centre of the first compression to the centre of the fifth compression is 2.0 m. The wavelength is:
x: From the first to the fifth compression there are 4 wavelengths, so λ = 2.0/4 = 0.5 m. Dividing by 5 (0.4 m) is the usual mistake.

q: As a progressive wave passes, which quantity for a particular particle of the medium keeps changing with time, while its amplitude stays constant?
o: The time period of its vibration
x: Displacement is the particle's distance from its mean position at a given instant, so it changes continuously between +A and −A. Amplitude is the fixed maximum value of that displacement.

q: A particle of a medium completes 120 vibrations in one minute as a wave passes. The time period of the wave is:
x: Frequency = 120/60 = 2 Hz, so T = 1/f = 0.5 s. Using 120 vibrations per second by mistake gives 0.0083 s.

q: The velocity of a progressive wave means:
o: The maximum speed of a vibrating particle of the medium
The speed at which particles of the medium travel away from the source
The speed with which the disturbance, such as a crest, moves forward through the medium
The number of waves produced per second
x: Wave velocity is the distance moved by the wave form per unit time (v = fλ). It is different from particle velocity, which changes continuously as each particle vibrates.

q: Two particles on a rope carrying a progressive transverse wave are half a wavelength apart. When one of them is at a crest, the other is:
o: At its mean position, moving up
At its mean position, moving down
x: Points λ/2 apart vibrate in opposite phase (phase difference π). So when one is at a crest, the other is at a trough.

q: A wave has a speed of 300 m s⁻¹ and a frequency of 100 Hz. Its wavelength is:
x: λ = v/f = 300/100 = 3 m. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 30 000 m.

q: A dolphin's click has a wavelength of 1.5 cm in sea water, where sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the click is:
x: f = v/λ = 1500/0.015 = 1 × 10⁵ Hz (ultrasound). Forgetting to change 1.5 cm into 0.015 m gives 1000 Hz.

q: A wave travels at 12 m s⁻¹ and has a wavelength of 3 m. The time period of the wave is:
x: f = v/λ = 12/3 = 4 Hz, so T = 1/f = 0.25 s. Stopping at 4 gives the frequency, not the period.

q: Water waves of wavelength 2 m travel at 4 m s⁻¹ in deep water. They move into shallow water, where their speed falls to 2 m s⁻¹. Their wavelength in the shallow water is:
x: The frequency does not change: f = 4/2 = 2 Hz. In shallow water λ = v/f = 2/2 = 1 m.

q: In a ripple tank, a dipper vibrates at 10 Hz. The distance from the first crest to the sixth crest is 10 cm. The speed of the ripples is:
x: Six crests span 5 wavelengths, so λ = 10/5 = 2 cm. v = fλ = 10 × 2 = 20 cm s⁻¹.

q: A boat bobs up and down 15 times per minute on sea waves whose crests are 8 m apart. The speed of the waves is:
x: f = 15/60 = 0.25 Hz, so v = fλ = 0.25 × 8 = 2 m s⁻¹. Forgetting to change minutes to seconds gives 120.

q: Yellow light has a wavelength of 600 nm in a vacuum. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, its frequency is:
Which of the following is NOT carried from place to place by a progressive water wave?
x: A progressive wave carries energy and the disturbance forward, and can carry a signal. The water particles only vibrate about their mean positions; there is no net transport of water.

q: The intensity of a wave is defined as:
o: The energy carried per unit time per unit area perpendicular to the direction of travel
The maximum displacement of the particles
The number of waves passing a point per second
x: Intensity is power per unit area, measured in W m⁻². For a given wave it increases with the square of the amplitude.

q: For a mechanical wave in a given medium, the energy carried is proportional to f²A², where f is the frequency and A the amplitude. If f is doubled and A is halved, the energy carried becomes:
x: New energy ∝ (2f)²(A/2)² = 4f² × A²/4 = f²A². The two changes cancel.

q: A small source sends sound out equally in all directions in open air, with no energy lost. At 2 m from the source the intensity is I. At 4 m from the source the intensity is:
x: The same power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr². Doubling r makes the area four times as large, so the intensity becomes I/4.

q: A wave's energy varies as the square of its amplitude. By what factor must the amplitude increase for the wave to deliver 9 times the energy, with frequency unchanged?
x: Energy ∝ A², so the amplitude must increase by √9 = 3. A factor of 9 in amplitude would give 81 times the energy.

q: In a progressive transverse wave on a string, the particles that have the greatest kinetic energy at a given instant are those:
o: Halfway between the mean position and a crest
x: A vibrating particle moves fastest as it passes through its mean position, so its kinetic energy is greatest there. At crests and troughs it is momentarily at rest.

q: The energy carried by a progressive wave moves through the medium at:
o: The maximum speed of the particles
Zero speed, since energy stays at the source
The speed of light, whatever the wave
x: Energy is handed on from particle to particle as the disturbance advances, so it travels at the wave speed v = fλ. Particle speed is a different quantity.

q: Light waves are:
x: Light consists of electric and magnetic fields vibrating perpendicular to the direction of travel, so it is a transverse electromagnetic wave. It can be polarised, which confirms this.

q: A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth along the same line as the wave travels is called:
x: In a longitudinal wave the particle vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions. In a transverse wave they are perpendicular to it.

q: After an earthquake, transverse seismic waves (S-waves) are not detected on the far side of the Earth, but longitudinal waves (P-waves) are. This suggests that part of the Earth's core is:
x: Transverse waves need a medium that resists sideways (shear) deformation, which a liquid cannot do, while longitudinal waves pass through liquids. Empty space would block the P-waves as well.

q: In a longitudinal wave, compressions correspond to which feature of a transverse wave?
x: Compressions are regions of maximum crowding, matching the crests of a transverse wave; rarefactions match the troughs. A wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions.

q: Which of the following can carry both transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves?
x: Solids resist both compression and sideways shear, so they carry both kinds of wave. Gases and liquids in bulk carry only longitudinal waves.

q: Dolphins use ultrasound under water. These ultrasound waves are:
x: Ultrasound is sound of very high frequency, so like all sound in a fluid it is a longitudinal mechanical wave. Electromagnetic waves are always transverse.

q: In which type of wave do the pressure and density of the medium rise and fall from point to point along the wave?
x: A longitudinal wave is a train of compressions (high pressure and density) and rarefactions (low pressure and density). A string wave displaces particles sideways, and light needs no medium.

q: In general, sound travels:
o: Fastest in gases and slowest in solids
Fastest in liquids and slowest in solids
At the same speed in solids, liquids and gases
Fastest in solids and slowest in gases
x: Solids are far more elastic than liquids, and liquids far more than gases, which outweighs their greater density. So sound is usually fastest in solids and slowest in gases.

q: The speed of sound in air calculated from Newton's formula was found to be:
o: About 16% less than the measured value
About 16% more than the measured value
Exactly equal to the measured value
x: Newton's formula gives about 280 m s⁻¹ at STP, while experiment gives about 332 m s⁻¹. The shortfall of roughly 16% was later explained by Laplace.

q: Aluminium has Young's modulus 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa and density 2.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³. The speed of longitudinal sound waves in an aluminium rod is:
x: v = √(E/ρ) = √(7.0 × 10¹⁰ / 2.8 × 10³) = √(2.5 × 10⁷) = 5000 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 2.5 × 10⁷.

q: Newton's formula gives the speed of sound in a gas of density 2.5 kg m⁻³ as 200 m s⁻¹. The pressure of the gas is:
x: From v = √(P/ρ), P = v²ρ = (200)² × 2.5 = 4 × 10⁴ × 2.5 = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Not squaring v gives 500 Pa.

q: For longitudinal sound waves along a thin solid rod, the modulus E in v = √(E/ρ) is:
o: The bulk modulus of the surrounding air
The shear modulus of the material
The pressure of the surrounding air
x: In a thin rod the material is stretched and compressed along its length, so Young's modulus applies. For a gas or liquid the bulk modulus is used instead.

q: Two solids have the same density, but the elastic modulus of one is 4 times that of the other. The speed of sound in the stiffer solid is:
x: v = √(E/ρ); with ρ the same, v ∝ √E, so 4 times the modulus gives √4 = 2 times the speed.

q: A ship's sonar sends a pulse of sound down to the sea bed. The echo returns after 2.0 s. If sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in sea water, the depth of the sea is:
x: The pulse travels down and back, so depth = (1500 × 2.0)/2 = 1500 m. Forgetting to halve gives 3000 m.

q: Laplace assumed that the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave in air obey:
x: Laplace treated the changes as adiabatic, for which PVᵞ = constant. PV = constant is Boyle's law, the isothermal assumption made by Newton.

q: Helium (γ = 1.67) and nitrogen (γ = 1.40) are compared at the same pressure and the same density. According to Laplace's formula, sound travels:
o: Faster in nitrogen, because its γ is smaller
At the same speed in both, because P and ρ are the same
Faster in helium, because its γ is larger
Faster in nitrogen, because its molecules are heavier
x: v = √(γP/ρ); with P and ρ equal, v ∝ √γ, so the gas with the larger γ (helium) carries sound faster.

q: Air at a certain temperature has density 1.4 kg m⁻³ when its pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Taking γ = 1.4 for air, Laplace's corrected value for the speed of sound is about:
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 10⁵ / 1.4) = √(10⁵) ≈ 316 m s⁻¹. Leaving out γ (Newton's formula) gives about 267 m s⁻¹.

q: For a certain gas, Newton's formula gives the speed of sound as 300 m s⁻¹, while Laplace's formula gives 390 m s⁻¹. The value of γ for this gas is:
x: v(Laplace)/v(Newton) = √γ, so √γ = 390/300 = 1.3 and γ = 1.3² = 1.69. Forgetting to square gives 1.30.

q: The adiabatic bulk modulus of air is larger than its isothermal bulk modulus. The reason is that in an adiabatic compression:
o: The temperature falls, so the air becomes easier to compress
The temperature rises, so the pressure rises more for the same decrease in volume
Heat flows in from the surroundings, keeping the temperature fixed
The density of the air stays constant
x: In a rapid (adiabatic) compression no heat escapes, so the air warms and its pressure rises more than in an isothermal compression. A larger pressure rise for the same volume change means a larger modulus, γP instead of P.

q: For any gas, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is:
o: Less than 1, because Cv is larger than Cp
Greater than 1, because Cp is always larger than Cv
x: At constant pressure some of the heat supplied also does work as the gas expands, so Cp > Cv and γ > 1. That is why Laplace's speed √(γP/ρ) is larger than Newton's √(P/ρ).

q: Laplace's correction to Newton's formula concerned Newton's assumption about:
o: The density of air at STP
The thermal conditions of the compressions and rarefactions
The frequency of the sound wave
The amplitude of the sound wave
x: Newton assumed the changes were isothermal; Laplace showed they are adiabatic, so the elastic modulus should be γP instead of P.

q: A sound is made outdoors on a hot afternoon and again at dawn, when the air is cooler. Other conditions being equal, the sound travels faster:
o: At dawn, because cool air is denser
At the same speed both times
In the hot afternoon, because the air temperature is higher
At dawn, because sound carries better in still air
x: The speed of sound in air increases with temperature (v ∝ √T in kelvin), so it is faster in the warmer afternoon air.

q: The speed of sound in air at −73 °C is 280 m s⁻¹. At 527 °C it will be:
x: In kelvin the temperatures are 200 K and 800 K, a ratio of 4. Since v ∝ √T, the speed doubles to 560 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 1120.

q: At the same temperature, sound travels faster in helium than in argon (both monatomic, so with the same γ). The reason is that helium:
o: Has a much larger molar mass
Has a much smaller molar mass, so it is less dense at the same pressure
Is a better conductor of heat
Exerts a higher pressure at the same temperature
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M). At the same T and γ, the gas with the smaller molar mass (helium, 4 g mol⁻¹, against 40 for argon) carries sound faster.

q: Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in still air. A steady wind blows at 10 m s⁻¹ from a source towards a listener. The speed of the sound relative to the ground, on its way to the listener, is:
x: Sound moves at 340 m s⁻¹ through the air, and the wind carries the air towards the listener, so relative to the ground the speeds add: 340 + 10 = 350 m s⁻¹.

q: If v₀ is the speed of sound in air at 0 °C, the speed at t °C is:
x: v ∝ √T with T = 273 + t in kelvin, so v = v₀√((273 + t)/273) = v₀√(1 + t/273). Leaving out the square root, or using t in °C directly, is wrong.

q: A siren emits a note of fixed frequency 1000 Hz. As the air warms from 0 °C to 30 °C, the wavelength of the sound in the air:
o: Decreases, because the speed rises while the frequency stays the same
Increases, because the speed rises while the frequency stays the same
Stays the same, because the frequency is fixed
Decreases, because warm air is less dense
x: The speed of sound rises with temperature, while the frequency is fixed by the siren. So λ = v/f increases.

q: A wave of amplitude 7 mm and a coherent wave of amplitude 3 mm overlap so that a crest of one always falls on a trough of the other. The amplitude of the resulting vibration is:
x: Crest on trough means opposite phase, so the displacements subtract: 7 − 3 = 4 mm. Complete cancellation would need equal amplitudes.

q: Waves from two sources reach a point with a phase difference of 2π. How much farther has one wave travelled than the other?
x: A path difference of one wavelength corresponds to a phase difference of 2π. Half a wavelength would give π.

q: Light from two separate ordinary lamps falling on a screen does not produce a visible interference pattern. The main reason is that the lamps:
o: Are not coherent, since their phase difference changes randomly
Emit light of exactly the same frequency
x: Ordinary lamps emit light in random bursts, so the phase difference between them keeps changing and any pattern shifts too fast to see. A steady pattern needs coherent sources.

q: When two coherent waves superpose, whether the result at a point is a maximum or a minimum depends on:
o: The phase difference between the waves at that point
The speed of the waves only
The direction in which the observer faces
x: In phase (0, 2π, ...) gives a maximum and opposite phase (π, 3π, ...) gives a minimum. The phase difference at each point fixes the type of interference there.

q: Two coherent sources oscillate exactly out of step with each other (antiphase) and send out waves of equal amplitude. At a point that is one wavelength farther from one source than from the other, the waves:
o: Give an amplitude equal to that of one wave
Give a maximum only if the sources are far apart
x: A path difference of λ adds a phase difference of 2π, which changes nothing, so the waves arrive with the sources' own phase difference of π. Equal amplitudes in opposite phase cancel.

q: In Young's double-slit experiment, light from a single source passes through two narrow slits. The two slits act as coherent sources because:
o: They are very close to the screen
They let through light of different colours
Both receive light from the same source, so their phase difference stays constant
They are lit by two separate lamps
x: Both slits are lit by the same wavefront, so any change in the source affects both equally and their phase difference stays fixed. That is what makes them coherent.

q: Two coherent sources vibrate in phase and send waves of equal amplitude A to a point P with a path difference of 2λ. The amplitude at P is:
x: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives constructive interference, so the amplitudes add to 2A. The intensity, not the amplitude, becomes 4 times that of one wave.

q: Two loudspeakers driven in phase by one generator produce sound of wavelength 2 m. Which of the following path differences gives a loud sound?
x: Loud (constructive) points have path difference nλ: 0, 2, 4, 6 m. 1, 3 and 5 m are odd multiples of λ/2 = 1 m, which give quiet points.

q: A tuning fork of 512 Hz sounded with a second fork gives 6 beats per second. The frequency of the second fork could be:
x: Beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂|, so the second fork is 6 Hz above or below 512 Hz. Halving the difference to 3 Hz is a common mistake.

q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 300 Hz and 302 Hz are sounded together. The time between two successive loud sounds (waxings) is:
x: Beat frequency = 302 − 300 = 2 Hz, so a loud sound comes every 1/2 = 0.5 s.

q: A fork of unknown frequency gives 4 beats per second with a 256 Hz fork. When the prongs of the unknown fork are filed slightly, which raises its frequency, the beats drop to 2 per second. The original frequency of the unknown fork was:
x: It was either 252 Hz or 260 Hz. Raising 260 Hz would increase the beats, so it must have been 252 Hz, rising towards 256 Hz to give fewer beats.

q: Two loudspeakers driven in phase emit sound of frequency 510 Hz; the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. At a point where the path difference is 1.0 m, there is:
o: Constructive interference, since the path difference is 1.5λ
Constructive interference, since the path difference is λ
Destructive interference, since the path difference is λ/2
Destructive interference, since the path difference is 1.5λ
x: λ = 340/510 = 2/3 m, so 1.0 m = 1.5λ, an odd multiple of λ/2. The interference there is destructive.

q: Two musicians tune their instruments by playing the same note together and listening for beats. The instruments are in tune when:
o: The beats are as fast as possible
Exactly one beat is heard every second
The sound becomes twice as loud at every moment
x: The beat frequency equals the difference of the two frequencies. When the beats vanish, the difference is zero, so the notes match.

q: Two identical sound waves of equal amplitude meet at a point exactly out of phase. A listener at that point hears:
o: A sound of double the frequency
x: Equal waves in opposite phase cancel (destructive interference), so the point is quiet. The energy is redistributed to the loud points, not destroyed.

q: In a stationary wave, all particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate:
o: In phase with one another, with the same amplitude
In phase with one another, but with different amplitudes
Out of phase with one another, with the same amplitude
With phases that change steadily from particle to particle
x: Within one loop all particles move up together and down together, but the amplitude varies from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinode. A steadily changing phase is a feature of progressive waves.

q: A stationary wave is given this name because:
o: Its particles do not vibrate at all
It can exist only in a solid
It carries energy at a steady speed
Its wave pattern does not move along the medium
x: In a stationary wave the loops stay in place; the particles still vibrate, but the crests do not travel along the medium.

q: In a stationary wave, the energy of the vibrating medium is:
o: Stored within each loop, changing between kinetic and potential forms
Carried steadily along the medium at the wave speed
x: Because the two component waves carry equal energy in opposite directions, nothing flows along the medium. Within each loop energy changes between kinetic (string passing straight) and potential (string at its extreme shape).

q: Two progressive waves, each of frequency 200 Hz, travel in opposite directions on a string and form a stationary wave. The particles at an antinode vibrate with a frequency of:
x: Superposition does not change frequency: every particle of the stationary wave, including those at antinodes, vibrates at the frequency of the component waves.

q: Consider the particles of a string vibrating as a standing (stationary) wave. Which of these is true?
o: Each particle reaches its maximum displacement slightly after its neighbour
The particles at the nodes vibrate with the largest amplitude
All particles that are not at nodes reach their maximum displacement at the same instant
The wave pattern moves along the string at speed fλ
x: Particles within a loop are in phase and adjacent loops are in antiphase, so the whole string reaches its extreme shape at one instant. A gradual phase lag along the medium belongs to a progressive wave.

q: When a wave on a string reflects from an end tied to a rigid support, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π. As a result, the fixed end of the string is always:
x: The incident and reflected waves are in opposite phase at the fixed end, so their displacements always cancel there. The rigid support cannot move, so it is a node.

q: Two waves of the same frequency but amplitudes 3 mm and 2 mm travel in opposite directions along a string. The resulting standing wave pattern has:
o: Maximum amplitude 5 mm and minimum amplitude zero
Maximum amplitude 5 mm and minimum amplitude 1 mm
Maximum amplitude 6 mm and minimum amplitude zero
Maximum amplitude 3 mm and minimum amplitude 2 mm
x: Where the waves always meet in phase the amplitude is 3 + 2 = 5 mm; where they always meet in opposite phase it is 3 − 2 = 1 mm. True nodes of zero amplitude need equal amplitudes.

q: Which description fits an antinode of a stationary wave?
o: A point where the displacement is always zero
A point where the particles never move
A point where the amplitude of vibration is maximum
A point where the wave changes its frequency
x: At an antinode the particles vibrate with the largest amplitude. The point of zero displacement at all times is a node.

q: In a stationary sound wave in air, a displacement antinode is a point where the variation of pressure is:
x: Where the air particles move most, the layers on both sides move together, so the air there is neither squeezed nor stretched and its pressure does not vary. Pressure nodes coincide with displacement antinodes.

q: In a stationary wave, the distance from the first antinode to the fifth antinode is 80 cm. The wavelength is:
x: Adjacent antinodes are λ/2 apart, and from the first to the fifth there are 4 gaps: 4 × λ/2 = 80 cm, so λ = 40 cm.

q: Waves of speed 24 m s⁻¹ and frequency 60 Hz form a stationary wave on a string. The distance between adjacent nodes is:
x: λ = v/f = 24/60 = 0.4 m, and adjacent nodes are λ/2 = 0.2 m apart. 0.4 m is the full wavelength.

q: A small folded paper rider is placed on a stretched wire vibrating in a stationary wave. The rider is thrown off when it is placed at:
x: The rider is thrown off where the wire vibrates with the greatest amplitude, at an antinode. At a node (including the fixed ends) the wire does not move, so the rider stays.

q: Two nodes of a stationary wave are 2λ apart. How many antinodes lie between them?
x: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, so a distance of 2λ holds 4 loops, each with one antinode at its centre.

q: In its fundamental mode, a string held at both ends has how many nodes and antinodes, including the ends?
x: The fundamental is a single loop: a node at each fixed end and one antinode in the middle.

q: A string 0.9 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in three loops at 300 Hz. The speed of the waves on the string is:
x: Three loops make 1.5 wavelengths, so λ = 0.9/1.5 = 0.6 m. v = fλ = 300 × 0.6 = 180 m s⁻¹.

q: Transverse waves move at 160 m s⁻¹ on a sitar wire whose vibrating length is 0.4 m. If the wire vibrates in two loops, its frequency is:
x: Two loops make one whole wavelength, so λ = 0.4 m and f = v/λ = 160/0.4 = 400 Hz. This is the second harmonic; the fundamental is 200 Hz.

q: A thicker string has 4 times the mass per unit length of a thinner one. Both have the same length and tension. The fundamental frequency of the thicker string is:
o: Twice that of the thinner string
Half that of the thinner string
One quarter that of the thinner string
The same as that of the thinner string
x: f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), so f ∝ 1/√μ. Four times the mass per unit length gives half the frequency.

q: A guitarist presses a string against a fret, shortening its vibrating length while the tension stays the same. The note produced:
o: Has the same frequency but is louder
Has the same frequency but a longer wavelength in air
x: The fundamental frequency is v/2L, and the wave speed on the string is unchanged. A shorter length L therefore gives a higher frequency.

q: A stretched string has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz. Its vibrating length is halved and its tension is made 4 times as large. Its new fundamental frequency is:
x: f ∝ √T / L. Halving L doubles f, and 4 times the tension doubles it again: 100 × 2 × 2 = 400 Hz.

q: The second harmonic of a stretched string is 240 Hz. The frequency of its fourth harmonic is:
x: The fundamental is 240/2 = 120 Hz, so the fourth harmonic is 4 × 120 = 480 Hz.

q: A pipe open at both ends can produce:
o: All harmonics, both odd and even
x: With an antinode at each open end, any whole number of half-wavelengths fits, so an open pipe gives all harmonics. A pipe closed at one end gives only odd ones.

q: A pipe open at both ends sounds its fundamental note, of wavelength 1.6 m. Neglecting end correction, the length of the pipe is:
x: For an open pipe the fundamental has λ = 2L, so L = 1.6/2 = 0.8 m. 0.4 m would apply to a closed pipe (λ = 4L).

q: An organ pipe of length 0.85 m has one end closed. Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹. Ignoring end correction, what is the lowest frequency above the fundamental that it can sound?
x: Fundamental f₁ = v/4L = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz. A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics, so the next one is 3 × 100 = 300 Hz, not 200 Hz.

q: On a hot day the temperature of the air inside an organ pipe rises. The frequency of the note produced by the pipe:
o: Increases, because the speed of sound increases
Stays the same, because the length is fixed
x: The wavelength is fixed by the pipe length, but the speed of sound rises with temperature, so f = v/λ increases.

q: A simple flute is modelled as a tube 0.85 m long, open at both ends. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ and ignoring end effects, its first overtone has a frequency of:
x: Fundamental f₁ = v/2L = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. An open tube gives all harmonics, so the first overtone is 2 × 200 = 400 Hz; 600 Hz would be the next one after that.

q: An organ builder wants a stopped pipe (closed at one end) to give the same lowest note as an open pipe 1.2 m long. Ignoring end correction, the stopped pipe should be:
x: Open pipe: f = v/2L = v/2.4. Closed pipe: f = v/4L'. Setting them equal gives 4L' = 2.4 m, so L' = 0.6 m.

q: A pipe closed at one end is sounding its first overtone. Including the ends, the air column has:
x: The first overtone of a closed pipe has L = 3λ/4: a node at the closed end, then an antinode, a node, and an antinode at the open end.

q: Three waves overlap at a point. At one instant their displacements there are +4 mm, −1 mm and +2 mm. The resultant displacement is:
x: By the principle of superposition the displacements add with their signs: 4 − 1 + 2 = +5 mm. Ignoring the sign of −1 mm gives +7 mm.

q: Two people talk at the same time in a room, and a listener can still pick out each voice. This is possible because:
o: Sound waves from one person absorb those of the other
Only one sound wave can exist in the air at a time
Sound waves pass through each other and continue unchanged
Sound waves from different people cancel completely
x: When waves overlap their displacements simply add, and after crossing each wave carries on with its own form. So each voice reaches the listener unaltered.

q: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves meet at a point, the quantity that is added, taking signs into account, is:
x: Superposition adds the displacements of the individual waves at each instant. Intensities and energies are not simply added, which is why destructive interference can occur.

q: A wave of amplitude 3 mm overlaps with a coherent wave of amplitude 4 mm. Depending on the point, the combined vibration has different sizes. Which value is impossible for the combined amplitude?
x: The combined amplitude ranges from 4 − 3 = 1 mm (opposite phase) to 4 + 3 = 7 mm (in phase). 8 mm is outside that range; 5 mm occurs at an intermediate phase difference.

q: At a certain instant, the resultant displacement at a point where two waves overlap is zero. This means that at that instant:
o: Both waves have stopped at that point
The two individual displacements are equal and opposite
Neither wave has reached that point
The two waves have destroyed each other's energy
x: Superposition adds the displacements, so a zero total means they are equal in size and opposite in sign. Both waves are still present and carry on afterwards.

q: The bright and dark fringes seen in Young's double-slit experiment are produced by:
o: Superposition of light waves from the two slits
Reflection of light from the edges of the slits
Absorption of light by the screen
Refraction of light in the air
x: Light from the two slits superposes on the screen: in-phase arrival gives bright fringes and opposite-phase arrival gives dark fringes.

q: Two waves overlap at a point. One gives a displacement of +5 mm there, and the resultant displacement is +1 mm. The displacement due to the other wave is:
x: Resultant = sum of displacements, so the other wave gives 1 − 5 = −4 mm.

q: Which of the following motions is NOT simple harmonic?
o: A mass oscillating on a light spring
A simple pendulum swinging through a small angle
The projection on a diameter of a point moving uniformly round a circle
A ball bouncing up and down on a hard floor
x: For SHM the restoring force must be proportional to displacement from a mean position. A bouncing ball feels only its constant weight between impacts, so its motion is periodic but not SHM.

q: A mass oscillating on a spring has a time period T. If the mass is made 4 times as large with the same spring, the period becomes:
x: T = 2π√(m/k), so T ∝ √m. Four times the mass gives √4 = 2 times the period.

q: The amplitude of a simple pendulum's swing is reduced from 4° to 2°. Its time period:
x: For small swings T = 2π√(l/g), which does not depend on the amplitude. Only the length and g decide the period.

q: A particle performs SHM with angular frequency 4π rad s⁻¹. Its time period is:
x: T = 2π/ω = 2π/4π = 0.5 s. Its frequency is 2 Hz.

q: A body in SHM passes through its equilibrium (mean) position. At that moment:
o: Its speed is zero and its acceleration is maximum
Both its speed and its acceleration are maximum
Its speed is maximum and its acceleration is zero
Both its speed and its acceleration are zero
x: At the mean position the displacement is zero, so the acceleration (∝ displacement) is zero, while all the energy is kinetic, so the speed is maximum.

q: A 1 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Its total energy is:
x: Total energy = ½kx₀² = ½ × 100 × (0.1)² = 0.5 J. Leaving out the ½ gives 1 J.

q: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 21%. Its time period increases by:
x: T ∝ √l, so the new period is √1.21 = 1.1 times the old one, an increase of 10%.

q: When SHM is represented as the projection of a point moving uniformly round a circle, the time period of the SHM equals:
o: The time for half a revolution
The time for one complete revolution of the point
The time for a quarter of a revolution
x: In one revolution the projection moves from one end of the diameter to the other and back, completing one full oscillation.

q: A spot on a turntable makes 2 rotations every second, and its shadow on a wall performs SHM. The angular frequency of the shadow's motion is:
x: The angular frequency of the SHM equals the angular velocity of the rotating point: ω = 2πf = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹.

q: The projection of a uniformly rotating point on a diameter passes through the centre of the circle. At that moment the speed of the projection is:
o: Half the speed of the rotating point
Twice the speed of the rotating point
Equal to the speed of the rotating point
x: At the centre the rotating point's velocity is parallel to the diameter, so the projection moves with the full speed ωr. This is the maximum speed of the SHM.

q: A reference point turns at 10 rad s⁻¹ on a circle of radius 0.1 m. The greatest acceleration of its projection on a diameter equals the point's centripetal acceleration. Its value is:
x: a(max) = ω²r = 10² × 0.1 = 10 m s⁻². Using ωr gives 1, which is the maximum speed in m s⁻¹.

q: A particle's SHM is modelled by a point going round a circle once every 1.2 s. Starting from the middle of its path, how long does the particle take to reach an extreme position?
x: Going from the centre to one end corresponds to a quarter turn of the reference point, so it takes T/4 = 1.2/4 = 0.3 s.

q: A point P goes round a circle of radius 20 cm once every 6 s. It begins at one end of a diameter. How far from the centre is the foot of the perpendicular from P to that diameter 1 s later?
x: In 1 s P turns through 360°/6 = 60°, so the projection is at r cos 60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 cm. Using sin 60° gives 17.3 cm.
